title: This walking robot hand looks like a futuristic Thing from 'The Addams Family'
summary:
Halloween is just around the corner, which makes it a good time to meet an Addams Family-inspired robot hand. Like Thing, the gothic sitcom's famous hand, this fully articulated hand can balance on its own fingertips and creep around. It goes a step further, too. It can tap keyboard keys, push small objects and even play a rudimentary computer game while balancing on its remaining fingers. It can also recover from a fall and lift itself up from a flat position.

This is not the first time engineers have tried a walking robot hand. Past efforts mostly worked, but they required altering the hand's structure, making each finger the same length so it could balance. Human hands are defined by their uneven fingers and opposite thumb. That asymmetry partly explains why we are so adept at handling many tools, but it is not well suited for upright walking.

A team of engineers from the Soft Robotics Lab at ETH Zurich in Switzerland set out to solve that problem, as they describe in a recent preprint, which is a paper that has not undergone peer review or been accepted for publication in a scientific journal. The team started with an off-the-shelf mechanical hand designed for humanoid robots, with five fingers and 20 actuated joints. They mounted a battery, several motion sensors and a tiny computer near where the hand would normally connect to a wrist. With these additions, the whole thing weighs 1.8 pounds.

The team trained the hand in a simulation environment using reinforcement learning, where the software rewarded the hand every time it correctly balanced on its uneven fingers. Every finger was assigned its own target position, so where and when each one moved varied depending on the task.

In real-world field tests, the hand traversed 14 different indoor and outdoor environments, crossing carpet, gravel, grass and metal with a springy, spider-like gait. It could also balance on several fingers while using the others to push a small cube forward. In testing, it correctly hit keys 29 out of 32 times while typing. It was even able to play the puzzle-solving video game Sokoban by pressing the correct arrow keys in sequence.

The team notes that these abilities may serve a purpose beyond a Halloween decoration. In the future, humanoid robots working in cramped areas could reach toward a spot they cannot get to, detach their hand, and send it off to retrieve an item. "Giving robotic hands their own mobility could make future robots more versatile in the spaces and interfaces built for people," the researchers write in the paper.
why_it_matters: The work explores how robots could handle spaces and tools made for people. It is only described in a preprint so far, so other scientists have not yet reviewed it.

keywords.explanation: Having joints that let every part move.
Having sides or parts that are not the same.
A paper that has not gone through peer review.
Training software by rewarding correct actions.
Robots built to look and move somewhat like people.

questions.question: Why did past walking robot hands change finger lengths?
options: Equal fingers helped the hand balance
They wanted the fingers to match a person's
It made the hand easier to build
Longer fingers made the hand lighter
questions.correct_answer: Equal fingers helped the hand balance

questions.question: What makes human hands good with tools but not with walking?
options: Their uneven fingers and opposite thumb
Their very large size and heavy weight
Their lack of joints in the fingers
questions.correct_answer: Their uneven fingers and opposite thumb

questions.question: What does a preprint mean in this story?
options: A paper that won a science prize
A paper written only by students
A paper that was printed in a famous magazine
A paper not yet peer-reviewed or accepted by a journal
questions.correct_answer: A paper not yet peer-reviewed or accepted by a journal

questions.question: How many actuated joints did the off-the-shelf hand have?
How many different environments did the hand cross in field tests?
What future use do the researchers suggest?
options: A robot that plays piano concerts
A robot detaching its hand to retrieve an item in a cramped area
A hand that cooks meals in restaurants
A hand that replaces human surgeons
questions.correct_answer: A robot detaching its hand to retrieve an item in a cramped area

background_read: Peer review is when other experts check a scientific paper before it is published.
